newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook-Shell's runs cut sparks hope.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook-Shell's runs cut sparks hope.

text.p: Singapore's gas oil market is consolidating around a new support level after breaking key levels to trade below $23.00-per-barrel last week but stability is tenuous as the prompt supply overhang continues to dominate, traders said on Monday.
Traders are hoping that news of Shell Singapore's plan to cut output by about seven percent for the rest of June will improve sentiment.

Prompt physical gas oil traded for the first time in over year at $23.00 on Tuesday but it has since recovered slightly to hover above the mark as fresh buying support emerged late week at this level.
Despite the new support, the market remains jittery as there are large amounts of prompt unsold gas oil in Singapore leading to speculation that more refiners will cut their output, traders said.

Already Esso Singapore had cut runs by 10 percent on May 27 at its 230,000 barrel-per-day refinery due to poor margins and high middle distillate stocks, a source close to the company told Reuters earlier.
A company spokeswoman for Esso however declined to make any comment.
On Monday Shell Singapore said it will cut output during the second half of the June to lower the June average ouput from 59,000 tonne per day (TPD) to 57,000 TPD.
As a result output for the rest of this month will be reduced by 4,000 TPD.
Traders hope that the cut will help alleviate the current high stocks in Singapore as middle distillate stocks have risen to their highest level in at least three and a half years.
Data from the Trade Development Board showed stocks in the week ending June 11 rose 993,000 barrels to 11.236 million barrels, the highest since at least January 1994.
The prompt overhang gripped the market mid-week when Singapore Refining Co was forced to ship some of its products for spot storage due to ullage problems at its refinery.
Distressed gas oil cargoes were sold down to a low of 40 cents below Singapore spot quotes on a free-on-board basis, compared to prevailing differential of about minus 10 cents, traders said.
Although the storage situation is no longer a problem, the market is concerned that if enduser demand does not surface soon the same problem will recur.
Traders said the problem of a supply glut will continue to dog the market unless China comes out to buy in a big way for July.

Regional oversupply are primarly due to the leftover of unsold arbitrage cargoes from the West. The cargoes totalling more than three million tonnes were shipped over a short space of two months arriving in late May to early July.
These cargoes on top of the normal regional output was too much for the market to cope, traders said.
"It takes a long time for the market to absorb so much product. I think things will only be back to normal in the third quarter if no new arbitrage cargoes come this way," one trader said.
China has already cut its imports in the second quarter drastically compared to the first quarter when it bought just over two million tonnes, traders said.
Chinese April gas oil imports at about 400,000 tonnes wer half of the March imports with May and June imports also expected to the close to the April levels.
As a result of these low purchases in the second quarter, traders are hoping that China will come back to buy large amounts in the third quarter.
Aside from China, the only other incremental July demand is seen from Indonesia due to maintenance shutdowns at the Balikpapan refinery.
The fuel oil market is treking a steady course at just under $100 per tonne with little change seen in the near future due to the absence of large export cargoes from the Middle East.
The gasoline market is picking up due to high domestic demand in South Korea and fresh demand from Indonesia due to the Balikpapan shutdown.
